title: Dating the Creole band; Papa Laine, LaRocca; Norwood Williams on Buddy Bolden
summary: Dates of the California Creole band, the Laine and Baquet bands against the Original Dixieland band, and Norwood Williams's 1939 account of Bolden.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: Around 1912 to 1914 all those dates had been given. That's the same band with George Barquet.
What kind of music do you think they were playing? Would it differ in any way from say what they were playing in the middle 20s?

I would doubt it myself just from the evidence of people's styles not changing that rapidly. I can't, we don't have any records of them. Actually the original Dixieland was the first to record. It might have been of course they always called it ragtime. A lot has been made like for instance in Brun's book on Nick LaRocca always made a big point of that. That they were the first ones to use the word jazz. But not, I'm not trying to say the colored people were first or anything of that kind in this particular case because Papa Lane will say the same that they played all the same tunes Tiger Rag. Incidentally, speaking of the Shiel Baquet who played with Papa Lane they played down here. Papa Lane had two or three so-called colored musicians who were so white that you couldn't tell. Shiel Baquet started passing down here of course when he played with Papa Lane. And he also played with Happy Schilling, a trombone player who's still living. We had a very good interview with him. He was so sick I didn't want to bother him when our Tulane project started. But we have a copy of his interview here which was arranged by Johnny Wiggs. Anyway, Happy Schilling used to laugh about his black and white orchestra. I think he tells that on the interview. And he had also a Shiel Baquet with his group. And both, I don't want to quote either one of them but I know they both seem to imply that Shiel Baquet was a pretty good composer and he used to help arrange they even thought he might have written some of those tunes which he probably never even claimed. But that might have been their first experience even with Tiger Rag. Possibly they talked like and all the Shiel Baquet would arrange those numbers sort of for us and neither one of those bands in those days bothered with music. And Shiel Baquet no doubt could read music and the... But anyway, Papa Lane especially and Mama Lane we'll call her will laugh at the idea of Nick LaRocca writing any of those tunes of course because they'll say, oh we played those so long before that Nick, well like Papa Lane tells us, Nick would come along and rehearse with us and sometime we'd take him out on a job we'd pay him the same as the others and we'd pay him the same as the others. Like it was a joke that they paid him but anyway they needed extra musicians and they'd pay him even if he couldn't play is what he was trying to say. and not that they were trying to run him down although there was no love lost between them I don't think because Nick made so many claims and they'd see him on television claiming that he originated everything and they started to make Mrs. Lane would make her sort of sick she'd get a little riled up but Jack Lane popped up and it seemed to bother him he'd just laugh at him say well let him talk let him talk so anyway some of those other bands both white and colored must have been playing at least as jazzy as the original Dixieland band sometimes it looks like Nick LaRocca's only point was that they used the word jazz on the records in all first and before that they were ragtime bands and therefore he originated jazz but I doubt myself that we have no evidence on records or anything else that can actually prove it they did play all these ragtime sheet pieces and there were a few blues maybe published of course before the original Dixieland certainly Handy had published a few blues and they probably weren't the first blues either Handy probably if you want to use the word stole more blues and things than Nick LaRocca did other ragtime pieces you might say but somebody had got them published and copyrighted sooner or later they would have been lost so I mean there's nothing to worry about the fact that they cashed in on them because somebody else would have if they hadn't so I can't see that it made much difference if you cashed in on them but to get on with Norwood Williams who was in that first Creole group we'll see here if I can figure out what he said in 1939 I learned from Bud Scott that Gigi I don't know how you would ever spell that I just spelled like G-E-E would say G-I-G-I yeah or it might have been G-I-G I don't know where that came from but anyway he lived in Watts down south of Los Angeles the suburb where they evidently had been the big Negro colony a lot of them from New Orleans Zoo Robertson lived down that way Jelly when he went out there I mentioned before he'd worked there at Leakes Lake an amusement park and Jelly's godmother lived down there too she was still living I never got to find her she'd been this woman he talks about sort of a voodoo queen not necessarily a queen but at least mixed up in voodoo so I went down and talked to him he was running a filling station and I took my copy of Jazzmen along to try to identify pictures and all and it says here they also had a photograph of the original Creole band hanging in the back room and they got it for me to look at it was in better condition than the one we borrowed from Bill Johnson's and it also I made a note it had no date on it Bill Johnson had had printed on his in hand printing 1912 but I'm quite skeptical of that date that band was actually together in that exact personnel at that time they possibly had played together most of those fellows down here as early as 1912 but I think 1912 was about the date that Dink and Bill went out to California and had maybe a string trio for a while and they sent for Keppard and Barkay and all a and here it says Williams was enthusiastic about Buddy Bolden remembering the Take It Away I played him that Jelly's the general record of that Buddy Bolden's Blues as Jelly called it Bolden's He said he had played with Bolden's He said he had played with Bolden's He had been a member of Bolden's Troubadours which is a name we've never heard of much anyplace else as being called the Bolden Troubadours He implied the Bolden Troubadours had traveled as if it might have been part of a show which we've never come across any information to confirm that He said Bolden had started in 1890 ! 1890 and had played in Audubon Park along with Ori and Bud Scott and Mutt the group that were out there he confirmed the story that Bolden got his jazz from hearing spirituals at church He said it was a Baptist church where the shouts were performed The shouts of course were sort of sometimes called ring shouts where they would even dance around in the rings not necessarily in here even over in the Carolinas and Georgia and all that through the south but it was rather a lively type not the slow type of spiritual I understand as say Go Down Moses it was a jumping type that they call Mahalia calls gospel music today It says it was at the Baptist church where the shouts were performed so energetically the church became nicknamed The Gymnasium Incidentally it reminds me out there that when I was there in those years around 1940 there was one church they told about there in Los Angeles they used to dance so much they knocked it off of the foundation One of the musicians told me that and another friend confirmed that Adrian Tucker They didn't knock it knock it down they just shifted off of the say the rock or brick foundation probably they just knocked it over got shaken so anyway they called this church where Bolden went which we've never been able to identify or locate here the Gymnasium Williams mentioned the tune I'm going when Jesus calls me as one that inspired Bolden I'm going when Jesus calls me I don't remember ever hearing it and we've never checked up we slipped up on those things really we should have been asking people I should have gone over these notes several years ago Williams told me what a powerful and expressive coronet Bolden was it may not be good English but it's the way it's written and how jazzy he was compared to Louis who might be regarded as a great novelty player Bolden really played jazz a lot of the old timers think that Louis played a lot of fast runs and
